administration and the county employees, my name is John Badesky. I have the honor to serve as your county administrator and today I also have the honor to introduce the recommended FY27 budget. I always want to make sure that I begin with recognition of the team we have.

This is highly influenced by our citizens, and I'm grateful for the turnout here today. budget. I think, as I say, this is a process. always a balance, there's always the meeting the needs that our citizens want and making sure that we balance that financial burden. the board's adopted budget which will ultimately serve this community for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. I want to talk a little bit about our budget. So while we are here talking about the fiscal year 27 budget that we're looking to recommend and introduce to you here today, we really look at planning horizons well beyond one year, and it's important to do that.

Why? When we're looking at those recommendations, we want to make sure that we're not recommending things to you that cannot be sustained due to funding projections and resources and forecasting. We also want to make sure that we look at staffing plans. as we recommend a position to you we want to make sure is it sustainable can we sustain that through five years but we also look beyond that we look at the 10-year horizon as we're doing debt service planning so as we're looking at the projects that we've done to date plus the next five years that we'll go over here today we want to make sure that we're balancing our debt not only with our fiscal policies with within the means that we have projected and then we do and i believe we're

now one of three counties in the commonwealth we actually do 25-year long-term capital planning and yes if i knew exactly what was going to happen in 25 years i might be serving a community in a different capacity but it's our job to also project those needs and understand what are those needs so as we're planning our communities and considering projects understanding where we're going to need our next school where are we going to need our next public safety facility and so on That's a critical part of our overall planning for our community.

But I want to step actually back right now and talk a little bit about what we've done collectively over the past five years. I think we all know that in the past five years we've been in a climate where property values have grown. That growth has also, while we've maintained our property rate, it does mean that some residents that had property growth and assessments have paid more over the years.

And I've had folks come up to me over the past couple of years and say, well, what did I get for my increase in taxes? And I think we really need to step back and understand where did we make those investments? Because there were periods of time, and we'll talk about it today, that we were unable to make those investments. So let's talk a little bit about that.

And today's budget, I think it's critical just to remind everybody, local governments have two primary services that we do for our community. And that's public education and public safety. Obviously, we provide human services and quality of life services and those kinds of things. But locally, charged localities have those two primary sources.

So I'm going to actually start with public education today. We are extremely proud of our public educators in this community and should be for many reasons. Today, you will hear from our superintendent about the outcomes they were able to again achieve and moving into the next year.

We should be extremely proud. We have one of the highest quality education systems, not only in the Richmond region, but in the Commonwealth. but we've had to make investments to be able to assure we could do that. In the past five years, we've made deliberate investments in our public school facilities.

As you're aware, we opened Ashland Elementary, Battlefield Park and Beaver Dam. We'll be opening this fall, Washington and Henry. We have a groundbreaking coming up here in the months to come. And the Center for Trades and Technology, we took that project on last year.

It was one of those projects that we came together on and said, hey, while it wasn't in plan, It's a need for our community and we're gonna step up and do what we can. We made investments of $182 million just in the past five years to meet the needs of these schools. That would have equated to about 17 cents of debt payments on those particular buildings.

And why did we do that? We did that because look at the years of those facilities and just give you a little bit of context. The average planned lifespan for a new school facility is about 50 years. The schools we have replaced in this plan, 93 plus years old, 90 years old, 96 years old, 88 years old.

This community has seen the value of those investments over the time. We've gotten our lifespans out of those buildings. But at some point, there becomes a decision point that we have to make. Does it make sense to continue to renovate and invest in old facilities and keep up with, you know, even though they've been added on to over the years, the cost of maintenance starts to outweigh what the value is of building a new facility.

and we made those decisions here and I'm going to talk about a few more that we have in the years to come. Buildings and quality environments are great components of public education and are critical to that success but at the end of the day it's the people. It's the people that are in those buildings making a difference in the lives of our children each day and that is our number one resource when we talk about the county and when I talk about the county it's not the schools and or the county we're collectively in this together to assure that success. and you'll see throughout this presentation, has changed dramatically. The competitiveness for the talent that local governments use every day has grown increasingly. dollars have gone over the past few years. I'm not going to spoil the superintendent's presentation. She has some wonderful results to share with you, but think about it. in our community and the expansion that we're about to undertake will allow us to expand our diesel equipment repair and welding program and also making sure that our teachers and their opportunities to learn and grow are addressed in the Professional Learning Center to continue to support the students in our community. serving that community well, reducing response times. Station four is underway now. We will be moving forward into station eight replacement this year. We use cash prudently to make sure that we're reducing that debt burden on our citizens our community in general but there are times that it makes sense to use debt but when we can use cash we do that and that's because the board has set those policies and has been prudent about putting money aside. Again, I go back to the people though. At the end of the day, the facilities are great.
